choices: A game in which players move one after another
A game played over and over forever, with payoffs received each time it is played
A game with infinitely many players
A game played once with infinite payoffs

stem: Why can collusion be sustained in an infinitely repeated game but not in a one-shot game?
choices: A player who defects can be punished in later periods
Cheating is illegal in repeated games
Payoffs are larger in repeated games
Players have no dominant strategy
explain: Slides p. 31: players that defect can be punished in subsequent periods.

stem: According to the slides, a player should defect when:
choices: The interest rate is zero
The rival has a dominant strategy
The one-time payoff from cheating is positive
The present value of cheating is greater than the present value of collusion

stem: What happens to the present value of a payment received every year forever when the interest rate rises?
choices: It falls
It stays the same
It becomes infinite
It rises
explain: PV = payment / i. A bigger i means a smaller PV: the future counts for less.

stem: True or false: A higher discount (interest) rate makes cheating on a collusive agreement more attractive.
choices: True
False
explain: True. The future punishment is worth less today, so the one-time gain from cheating weighs more.

stem: In the formula PV cheat = 15 + 2/i for Kellogg's, what does the 2 represent?
choices: The interest rate
The payoff each period after General Mills starts punishing
General Mills' payoff from colluding
The one-time gain from cheating
explain: After cheating, both advertise forever and Kellogg's earns 2 per period.

stem:
Kellogg's versus General Mills (slides p. 34):

| Kellogg's \ General Mills | Don't advertise | Advertise |
|---|---|---|
| Don't advertise | 12, 12 | -1, 15 |
| Advertise | 15, -1 | 2, 2 |

At i = 10%, what is the present value of colluding (not advertising) forever, counting this period's payoff?
Same Kellogg's game at i = 10%. What is the present value of cheating this period, then being punished forever?
Comprehension Quiz 9 Q6 numbers ($ billions): neither advertises 4 each; the lone advertiser 44; both advertise 0 each. At i = 12%, what is the present value of colluding?
explain: PV collude = 4 + 4/0.12 = 4 + 33.33 = 37.33. Cheating is worth 44 + 0/0.12 = 44, so Kellogg's defects.

stem: A firm earns $50 every year forever starting next year. At an interest rate of 20%, what is that stream worth today?
explain: Perpetuity: 50 / 0.20 = 250. (No payment today, so nothing is added.)

stem: Two airlines collude on a route and each earns $30 million per year. If one cheats it earns $55 million this year, then $10 million per year forever. At i = 25%, what is the present value of cheating?
explain: PV cheat = 55 + 10/0.25 = 55 + 40 = 95. (PV collude = 30 + 30/0.25 = 150, so they keep colluding.)

stem: Same airlines at i = 25%: collude 30 per year forever; cheat 55 once then 10 per year. Should an airline cheat?
choices: No: colluding is worth 150 and cheating 95
It cannot be determined without the rival's payoffs
Yes: 55 is more than 30
Yes: cheating is worth 150

stem: A firm's owner becomes very impatient and now discounts the future at 300% a year. What does this do to its collusive agreement with a rival?
choices: Forces the rival to cheat first
Has no effect
Makes collusion more stable
Makes cheating more likely, because future punishment is worth little to it
explain: With a high i, the future punishment term (payoff / i) shrinks.

stem: Two cereal firms have colluded on advertising for decades. Which change would most threaten that collusion?
choices: Interest rates fall
The game is expected to last forever
The one-time gain from cheating grows much larger
The punishment payoff falls
explain: A bigger temptation (cheat minus collude) raises the PV of cheating relative to colluding.
